content.text: Tell how the Great Fire of London began in September 1666.
Tell how wooden houses and strong winds helped the fire spread.
Tell how people used buckets, fire hooks and firebreaks.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 2 minutes. Read the account aloud. Ask pupils to say where and when the fire began, then have them tell a partner how the bakery’s ovens relate to the fire.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think the fire began in a church or started in the streets. Reinforce that it began in Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane, where the ovens used fire.

Background
The fire began in the early hours of 2 September 1666. Thomas Farriner was a baker to King Charles II.

content.text: The Great Fire of London started on 2 September 1666. It began in Thomas Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane, where bread ovens used fire.

reasons.head: Wood
reasons.line: Many houses had wooden frames that burned.

reasons.head: Gaps
reasons.line: Close houses let flames reach neighbouring buildings.

reasons.head: Wind
reasons.line: Strong winds blew flames towards other houses.

content.text: Many houses had wooden frames that burned.
Close houses let flames reach neighbouring buildings.
Strong winds blew flames towards other houses.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes. Pupils choose an answer independently, then explain their choice to a partner. Take a few responses and clarify why wind made nearby houses more at risk.

Answers
A: They blew flames towards houses.

Misconceptions
“They blew the flames out” suggests wind would put out the fire; strong winds can instead carry flames and sparks. “They kept flames burning upright” misses how wind pushes flames towards nearby buildings. The correct idea is that wind blew flames towards houses.

Background
Wind can carry sparks ahead of a fire, as well as push flames towards nearby buildings.

content.text: How did strong winds help the London fire spread?

slides.notes:
Running
About 2 minutes. Ask pupils to work in pairs to mime passing a bucket along a line. Then ask what might make this method difficult during a large fire.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think everyone threw water at once or that one bucket could stop the fire. Explain that passing buckets along a line helped move water to the people nearest the flames, but it was difficult to get enough water to control such a large fire.

Background
Leather buckets were useful because leather could hold water and was less likely to split than a wooden bucket. People also used other methods, including pulling down buildings.

content.text: People filled leather buckets with water. They passed buckets along a line and threw water onto the fire.

elements.alt: People pass leather buckets of water along a line to fight the Great Fire of London.
elements.name: Photo

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes. Use the picture to ask what the hook is doing. Pupils explain to a partner how pulling down timber near the flames might help.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think fire hooks were used to pour water or lift people. Explain that the hooked pole pulled parts of nearby houses down to remove material the fire could reach.

Background
Pulling down timber buildings was dangerous, but removing them could help create a gap between the flames and other houses.

content.text: Fire hooks were long poles with metal hooks. People used them to pull down parts of houses near flames.

elements.alt: A 1666 London fire-hook scene showing a long wooden pole’s curved metal hook pulling a timber from a house.
elements.name: Photo

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes. Read the meaning, then ask pupils to explain how a gap with fewer buildings could slow the fire. Take one or two answers.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think a firebreak is a barrier built to block flames, or that it means putting out the fire. Explain that it is a gap made by removing buildings, leaving fewer houses for the fire to reach.

Background
Some buildings were pulled down to make gaps, though this could be difficult and dangerous while the fire was spreading.

elements.alt: William Russell Birch - The Great Fire of London in the Year 1666
elements.name: Photo

content.text: People pulled down whole houses to make firebreaks. These gaps left fewer buildings for flames to reach and burn.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes. Ask pupils to trace the route flames might take from the burning houses. They explain why the cleared gap could help the row beyond it.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think the unburnt houses are safe simply because they are farther away. Point out that the gap separates them from the burning row, so flames have fewer buildings to reach across.

Background
A firebreak could reduce the chance of flames spreading from one row of timber buildings to another, but it did not guarantee that houses beyond it would remain safe.

elements.alt: An overhead reconstruction of a London street during the Great Fire of 1666, with burning timber houses ending at a wide cleared firebreak and an unburnt row beyond it.
elements.name: Photo

content.text: The firebreak separates burning houses from houses not burning.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Pupils answer both questions independently, then compare answers in pairs. Invite a few pupils to explain how the distance between houses matters.

Answers
1. A narrower street has houses closer together, so flames can reach the next wooden house more easily.
2. The gap leaves fewer buildings for flames to reach across, so houses beyond it may escape burning.

Misconceptions
Pupils may say the narrow street is safer because it is shorter, or that a firebreak puts out the fire. Focus them on the distance between wooden houses: a smaller gap makes it easier for flames to spread; a firebreak removes houses from the route.

Background
Timber houses packed close together gave a fire a ready path from building to building. Wind could make that spread more dangerous.

content.text: Two streets have wooden houses. Why might fire spread faster along the narrower street?
A street has a wide firebreak. Why might houses beyond the gap escape burning?

question.modelAnswer:
1. The houses are closer together, so flames can reach the next house more easily.
2. The gap leaves fewer buildings for the flames to reach and burn.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils answer all three from memory, then check their responses with a partner. Review each answer together.

Answers
1. September.
2. Pudding Lane.
3. Buckets.

Misconceptions
A wrong month shows pupils may not have retained the date; remind them the fire began on 2 September 1666. A different street name confuses the bakery’s location; it was Pudding Lane. “Houses” or “pumps” for the last answer misses the method taught here: people filled buckets with water.

content.text: In which month did the London fire begin?
What was the name of the street containing Farriner’s bakery?
What did people fill with water to fight flames?

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Pupils write a response to each situation independently. Ask them to include how each action could help, then take a couple of answers.

Answers
1. People could fill leather buckets with water, pass them along a line and throw the water onto the shed.
2. People could use fire hooks to pull down parts of the empty wooden house, making a gap that could help protect the houses beyond it.

Misconceptions
Pupils may suggest that buckets alone would stop any fire, or that fire hooks were used to throw water. Remind them that buckets carried water, while hooks pulled down timber; removing an empty house could create a gap to help protect others.

Background
These actions were different ways people tried to limit the fire: buckets put water on flames, while pulling down buildings could remove fuel from the fire’s path.

content.text: Water is nearby and a small shed burns. How could people use buckets?
Flames approach an empty wooden house. How could fire hooks help protect houses beyond it?

question.modelAnswer:
1. They could pass buckets of water along a line and throw the water onto the flames.
2. People could use fire hooks to pull down the house and help make a firebreak.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Pupils complete both exit-ticket answers independently. Collect their responses to check recall of the starting place and understanding of how wind spread the fire.

Answers
1. It started in Thomas Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane.
2. Strong winds could blow flames towards nearby houses, helping the fire reach buildings beyond those already burning.

Misconceptions
Pupils may name London generally instead of the bakery on Pudding Lane, or say wind put the fire out. Revisit the exact starting place and explain that wind could push flames towards other houses.

content.text: Where did the Great Fire start in September 1666?
Why could strong winds threaten houses beyond burning buildings?

question.modelAnswer:
1. Thomas Farriner’s bakery, Pudding Lane.
2. Strong winds could blow flames towards other houses and set them alight.
